name: Gynecomastia surgery

card.summary: Surgical removal of excess glandular and fatty chest tissue in men; the established medical route when enlargement persists, with documented complication risks and variable insurance coverage.
card.aka: Male breast reduction, gynecomastia correction, subcutaneous mastectomy
card.note: Surgical procedure with documented complications such as hematoma, asymmetry and altered sensation; often classed as cosmetic by insurers.

quick.overview:
Gynecomastia is enlargement of glandular breast tissue in males. Surgery removes that tissue, often combined with liposuction of surrounding fat, to flatten the chest contour. Reference sources describe it as the main treatment when the condition persists beyond about a year, is distressing, and has become fibrotic.

In appearance-focused communities it is discussed as a chest-contouring procedure, and clinical studies have examined its effect on quality of life, particularly in adolescents and young men.
quick.mechanism: Techniques described in the literature include subcutaneous mastectomy through a small incision around the areola, liposuction-assisted removal, and laser-assisted variants. The aim is to remove glandular tissue, which liposuction alone may not address.
quick.risks: Reported complications include hematoma, infection, seroma, asymmetry, altered nipple or breast sensation, visible scarring, contour irregularities and, rarely, nipple or areola necrosis. Many US insurers classify the procedure as cosmetic and deny coverage. Pubertal gynecomastia often resolves on its own, so surgery in teenagers is generally deferred.

lead: Gynecomastia surgery, also called male breast reduction, is a set of operations that remove excess glandular tissue and, often, fat from the male chest. Gynecomastia itself results from an altered balance between estrogen and androgen activity and can arise during puberty, in older age, with certain medications or illnesses, or without an identified cause [1].

Reference sources describe surgery as considered when enlargement has persisted for roughly a year or more, causes physical or psychological distress, and has become fibrotic, and as typically reserved for cases that do not respond to medication [1]. A professional body cited on Wikipedia calls surgery the most effective known treatment for the condition [1]. Published case series and database analyses have documented complication rates and patient-reported outcomes [2][3].

Clinical studies of the operation consist largely of observational series, comparisons of technique and quality-of-life questionnaires, plus a number of small registered trials of specific methods [4][5].

paras: Pubertal gynecomastia is common and usually regresses within one to three years, and reference sources note that surgery is generally postponed until puberty is complete [1]. A study of adolescents who underwent surgery at a Korean hospital notes that most adolescent cases resolve spontaneously within about three years, while persistent cases can affect psychological development [6].

In adults, persistent gynecomastia may follow medication effects, chronic illness, or hormone therapy. In men treated with hormone therapy for prostate cancer, large randomized studies reported gynecomastia in around half or more of patients, and it was cited as a leading reason for stopping therapy early [7]. Tissue removed during surgery is routinely sent for pathology, though its usefulness in adolescents has been questioned because breast cancer is rare in that group [1].

Described approaches include subcutaneous mastectomy, liposuction-assisted mastectomy, laser-assisted liposuction and laser-lipolysis without suction [1]. A systematic review has examined liposuction-assisted surgery through a minimal periareolar incision [8]. Registered trials have compared endoscopic and open surgery, periareolar excision versus a pull-through technique, modified Benelli procedures, and laparoscopic gland resection combined with nipple-areola complex lift [9][10][11][12][13]. A trial has also tested a radiofrequency-assisted device as an adjunct in gynecomastia surgery [14].

A prospective case-control study of 50 male patients (mean age about 25) used the SF-36 health questionnaire before and after surgery to assess quality of life and satisfaction [4]. A later study examined complications and quality of life after correction in adolescents and young men [5]. A national multi-institutional database analysis reviewed outcomes and complication rates in 204 pediatric and 1,583 adult cases [3].

Other work includes analyses of the characteristics and short-term surgical outcomes of adolescents who underwent surgery [6], reviews of insurance coverage criteria in the United States [15], and trials of anesthesia and bleeding-control methods used during gynecomastia surgery [16][17].

Reference sources list hematoma, wound infection, seroma, asymmetry, altered breast sensation, necrosis of the nipple or areola, visible or painful scarring and contour deformities as possible complications [1]. Large database analyses report complication rates for both adult and pediatric patients [3].

Many US insurers treat gynecomastia surgery as cosmetic and deny coverage, and published reviews have compared the criteria that insurers use [1][15]. In 2019 about 24,000 US men had the procedure, a 19 percent increase since 2000 [1]. In looksmaxxing and hardmaxxing communities it is discussed as one of the standard surgical options for chest appearance.
